Keywords: Bog Myrtle and Yarrow Gruit Blend
RagShortTexts: Archbishops monopolized herbal gruit mixtures, challenged by hopped beer allowing long.

Variants.Content: Northern European brewing underwent a commercial transformation. Ale had long been flavoured and preserved with gruit, a secret herbal blend of bog myrtle, yarrow, and wild rosemary whose sale was monopolised by prince-archbishops under the gruitrecht. Cultivated hops brought bitter compounds that slowed spoilage, so cask beer could be kept for months rather than weeks. That durability opened long-distance export along the Baltic sea lanes, and brewers in the Hanseatic towns began to produce beer as a cargo rather than a local drink. The shift weakened the revenue of the gruit monopolists and put new commercial power in the hands of the town councils that controlled the brewing trade.

Ecclesiastical magnates resisted hops to protect the gruit monopolies that paid their treasuries. Autonomous Hanseatic cities embraced hopped brewing, and beer casks became a main ballast cargo for northern shipping. A town council that licensed brewers had to weigh its tolls and excise against the rising demand of distant markets.
Gruit ale sours into vinegar in days. Hopped brews taste pleasantly bitter and remain clear in cellars throughout winter, shielding tavern goers from tainted ditch water.
